blocks.heading: Corporate Law Is Eight Kinds of Work
rows: Regulatory, compliance and data privacy
Reading a rule, turning it into a checklist, a policy and a training session for a company. Deadlines come from the law, not from a deal.
People who like rules, documents and steady process more than deal adrenaline.
Scalable
Fixed packages: a compliance audit, a policy pack, a monthly retainer for small and mid-size companies.
Startups and venture work
Founder agreements, fundraising documents, employee option plans and the first contracts of a young company. Broad, fast and often thin on process.
People who want business exposure early and can work without a big team around them.
Scalable with a business layer
Fractional or retainer counsel for several young companies at once.
Tax
Advising on how a deal or a structure is taxed, and supporting tax disputes. Heavy on numbers and statute.
People comfortable with both law and accounts, such as a BCom LLB graduate.
A tax advisory practice for business owners, usually after years inside a firm.
Intellectual property
Filing and protecting patents, trademarks and copyright, plus commercial IP agreements. Patent work often rewards a science or engineering first degree.
Detail-minded people, and graduates who already hold a technical degree.
A boutique IP firm that runs on filings, renewals and repeat clients.
Mergers, acquisitions and private equity
Due diligence, drafting deal documents and managing a closing checklist. Work arrives in surges tied to the deal calendar.
People who can hold detail under time pressure and accept long stretches of heavy hours.
Not so scalable
Later: independent deal advisory, once you hold client relationships of your own.
Banking and finance
Loan, security and financing documents, on the lender or the borrower side. Repeatable documents, large sums and strict timelines.
People who like structured, document-heavy work and are comfortable with finance terms.
Not so scalable
Later: lender-side or borrower-side advisory, or a move to a bank or fund legal team.

blocks.heading: Firm, In-House, Boutique: the Verdict By Route
rows: Top (Tier-1) law firm associate
Internship record, campus placement or a pre-placement offer, mostly from top National Law Universities and a few other colleges.
Best training and the highest early pay of any corporate route. Long hours in deal teams, and a very narrow top rung.
Not so scalable
After years of experience: a boutique firm or independent advisory.
Mid-size or boutique firm associate
Interviews and referrals. Less campus-driven, so work samples and internships carry more weight.
Often broader, earlier responsibility and a faster route to a client. Pay and brand are lower than the top tier.
Not so scalable
A natural stepping stone to your own boutique, because you meet clients sooner.
In-house at a large company or bank
Usually hired after some firm experience, though legal executive roles exist at the start.
You work for one business, closer to the decision. A lawyer who takes a full-time salaried job gives up the right to practise as an advocate in court.
Not so scalable
Later: independent advisory, if you leave the salary.
In-house at a startup or venture-backed company
Hired on skills and trust, not on college brand. Few seats, and many ask for experience.
Wide scope, little supervision and fast learning. Stability depends on the company.
Fractional counsel for other young companies once you have a track record.
Compliance, privacy and company secretary advisory
Skill-gated. Company secretary work has an ICSI exam ladder; privacy and compliance roles hire on proof.
Steadier hours and a clear paying problem. Entry is open, so a sector niche matters.
Scalable
Fixed-price audits and retainers sold directly to companies.
Your own boutique or independent counsel
Enrolment as an advocate if you want court work, plus a client base. Bar Council advertising rules limit how you find clients.
You set fees and can add juniors, but the first years can be thin without referrals.
The route is the business: niche, packages, referrals, repeat clients.

blocks.heading: Partner Track and Lateral Moves
rows: Associate
0 to 3 years
Drafting, diligence, checklists. You learn the documents.
Senior associate
3 to 5 years
You run parts of a deal and manage juniors.
Principal associate
5 to 7 years
You handle clients day to day. A common window for a lateral move.
Counsel or salaried partner
6 to 9 years
Senior and salaried, with no profit share and usually no vote.
Non-equity partner
8 to 11 years
A entry requirement of a few years before equity at many top firms.
Equity partner
9 to 13 years
Ownership: profit share, vote and downside risk. Expected to bring clients.

blocks.heading: Building a Boutique Business Layer
rows: Firm associate
The firm, funded by company clients.
Internship record, a writing sample and the interview. Later, a partner who vouches for you.
Explaining a legal risk to a non-lawyer in two plain sentences.
Offers or pre-placement offers per set of internship applications.
In-house lawyer
The employer.
Firm references, a clean record on past deals and a business-friendly style.
Saying yes with conditions, instead of a long list of risks.
Matters you closed without escalation.
Boutique or independent counsel
Referrals from accountants, company secretaries, bankers and former colleagues, plus a sample deliverable.
One clear offer with a price, and a follow-up routine with every referrer.
Enquiries that turn into a paid engagement, and clients who come back.
Compliance advisory
Companies facing a fixed legal deadline.
A sample checklist, a fixed-price audit and a client who will speak for you.
Packaging an audit as a product a manager can approve.
Audits that convert into a monthly retainer.
